rationale: Background EEG amplitude and spectrum vary a lot between neonates, and in the referential montage the channel maximum tends to pick up artifact or high-amplitude channels rather than the seizure. I now normalize each channel's log features against that channel's own median over the whole recording (no labels needed). The max/median across channels then measures how far a channel has risen above its own baseline, which should pick up focal seizures far more reliably. The raw max/median features stay in.

Switch from the referential montage to the clinical neonatal bipolar double-banana montage (18 derivations), with a 0.5–30 Hz band-pass filter, before computing the same features. The common-reference montage spreads artifacts and background across all channels and dilutes focal, low-amplitude seizures. Bipolar derivations bring out local rhythmic discharges, and the filter keeps line length from being driven by mains noise and DC drift.

Switch from the referential montage to the 18-channel neonatal bipolar double-banana montage before computing features. The shared reference spreads one signal across every channel and hides focal, low-amplitude neonatal seizures. Bipolar derivations cancel that common-mode signal and show local rhythmic discharges in the channel pairs over the seizure region, which should make the max-over-channels features more informative.

Background EEG amplitude and spectrum vary a lot between neonates, so absolute log-power and line-length thresholds don't carry over well from one neonate to another. I'm appending a robust per-recording standardised copy of each feature (subtract the recording's median, divide by its IQR; no labels used), so the GBM can respond to changes relative to each neonate's own background while keeping the absolute values.

I'm switching from the 19 referential electrodes to the clinical neonatal 18-channel bipolar double-banana montage, with a 0.5–30 Hz zero-phase band-pass filter. Neonatal seizures are focal and often low in amplitude. The bipolar derivations remove activity common to the reference and pick up local field gradients, so the per-channel max/median features should make focal rhythmic discharges stand out more clearly. The filter removes DC drift and high-frequency muscle and line noise that currently inflate line length and RMS.

I'm switching from the referential signals to the clinical neonatal bipolar double-banana montage (18 derivations), band-pass filtered to 0.5–30 Hz before computing the features. In referential recordings the shared reference adds common-mode activity and artifact to every channel. That inflates the max/median features and hides focal discharges, and bipolar derivations are the standard way to bring out those local rhythmic seizure patterns. Everything else stays the same, so any change in score comes from the montage alone.

I'm switching the features from the referential montage to the clinical neonatal double-banana bipolar montage (18 derivations), with a 0.5–30 Hz zero-phase Butterworth band-pass. Neonatal seizures are focal, so local potential differences between neighbouring electrodes should make them stand out, while reference noise, DC drift and line noise drop out. Without this, that noise dominates the max/median-over-channel features.

Neonatal seizures are focal and often low-amplitude. With a referential montage, activity at the shared reference and slow drift dominate the signal and hide local rhythmic discharges. Bipolar derivations cancel that shared activity and show what is happening locally, which is how clinicians read neonatal EEG.
